source_credit: Baltasar Gracián, The Art of Worldly Wisdom (1647; public-domain translation by Joseph Jacobs, 1892). Plain one-line maxims in our own words, one per maxim 1 to 300.

entries.text: Treat every customer talk as a skill. Practice it on purpose.
When you hire, check that they keep their word, not just their skill.
Do not announce a new plan until it works.
Knowing the problem is half the job. Act on what you learn.
Be so reliable that people choose to come back to you.
Give your people time to grow. Judge them by their progress.
When a worker has a better idea than yours, use it and give them credit.
When someone yells at you, stay calm. Decide after the heat passes.
If your trade is known for a bad habit, be known for the reverse.
A slow week passes. A bad name stays. Guard your name first.
Spend time with people who know more than you. Ask them real questions.
Talent is not enough. Teach new people a clear routine.
When a first offer looks too good, look again before you agree.
Bad news goes down easier when you say it calmly and show proof.
Keep smart helpers close. If you cannot pay them, make them friends.
Use what you know about people only to help them.
Stay steady with customers and crew. Keep rivals guessing.
Steady work each week beats rare bursts of genius.
Promise a little less than you can do. Then beat it.
When the timing is right for a move, use it before the chance closes.
Luck finds people who show up and keep trying. Be there.
Keep a few good examples ready. A short story teaches more than a lecture.
Fix small flaws fast. People notice them more than your big wins.
When your mind jumps to the worst case or the best case, check the facts.
When someone says they will think about it, ask what would help them decide.
Learn what each person on your team cares about. Lead them with that.
Do a few things very well instead of many things poorly.
Do not copy a trend because it is popular. Ask if it serves your customers.
Stay honest on the days it costs you money. That is the real test.
Skip cheap stunts and shady side deals. They stick to your name.
Keep clear of people who are always in trouble. Their mess spreads.
Use your power to make someone's bad day easier.
Hand off tasks others can do. Keep your time for choices only you can make.
Find what you are best at. Spend more of your hours there.
Think hard about big choices. Spend little time on small ones.
In a good month, fix what you put off. In a slow month, hold tight.
Skip the cutting jokes. One mean remark can end a good bond.
When a promotion works, plan its end before it fades.
Launch when it is good enough to help. Do not polish forever.
People like you for fair acts, not just skill. Treat your crew fairly.
Skip big words in ads and reports. Say what is true.
Lead by knowing the work and staying the same each day.
Argue hard plans in private with people you trust. Then explain the result plainly.
When you meet someone who thinks like you and does good work, keep in touch.
Watch for tricks from others. Keep your own deals clean.
When someone rubs you the wrong way, give them a fair hearing anyway.
When someone starts a fight in public, reply one time with the facts. Then drop it.
A nice front means nothing if the work behind it is weak.
Watch where people pause or frown. It shows what they really think.
Do the job right even when nobody will check it.
Before a big choice, put the options side by side and compare them.
When things break at once, keep your voice calm. People follow your tone.
Once you decide, act that day. Do not let it sit.
Be easy to deal with. When someone keeps taking advantage, stop it fast.
Some things take seasons to build. Measure your progress in months.
Write short checklists for bad days so the crew can act fast.
On safety work, do it right before you do it fast.
Do not pile every repair idea on a customer at once. Fix what matters today.
End every visit well. People remember the goodbye more than the hello.
Put calm, steady people in charge of hard calls, not just the fastest ones.
Be known for what customers care about most, like honest work.
Hire strong people and buy good tools. You get the blame for weak ones.
If you can be first at something useful, move early.
Only let news reach you that you can act on.
Raise your standards by studying great work. Do not nitpick everything.
People judge by the result. Get the job right, and never cut corners to get there.
Let customers see the good work you did, like a note on what you checked.
Speak up with a tip at the right moment. Many things fail because nobody tried.
If you say yes too fast when excited, sleep on it first.
When you must say no, say it kindly and point them somewhere useful.
Keep your rules steady so people know what to expect.
When stuck between two good options, choose one. Review it on a fixed day.
A light joke can ease a tense moment. Never use one to dodge a real question.
As you grow, stay easy to reach for your crew and customers.
Study the best in your field. Use their level to push your own work.
Joke now and then. Be serious about safety and price.
Change your tone to fit the person. Never change the facts.
Before a big change, test it small first.
Laugh off small mishaps. A cheerful boss keeps a long day moving.
When you hear about a problem from someone else, check the record before you act.
Refresh how you show up before people get used to you.
Do not squeeze every last hour or dollar. Pushing too hard turns good into bad.
You do not need to look perfect. Own your small mistakes in the open.
Read a harsh review for the true part. Fix it and thank them.
Do not push your message everywhere. Show up where it counts.
Fix a complaint fast, before it becomes the story people tell.
Keep learning outside your trade. It sharpens how you talk and think.
Let a small slip pass once it is fixed. Do not dig into every detail.
Once a month, check your past choices against how they turned out.
Keep a pace and habits you can hold for years.
If your gut says a deal is wrong, do not sign it.
A plain plan your team can follow beats a clever one they cannot.
Train people to cover more than one job. Work keeps moving when someone is out.
Keep learning so you always have more to offer than people expect.
Roll out changes in steady steps, not one big drop.
When in doubt, take the safe path.
A good name is hard to earn and easy to keep. Guard it daily.
In a deal, do not show how badly you want it.
Honest advice can look like a sales pitch. Show the proof and the reason.
Be the real thing, not just the image of it.
Do not let a single fan or critic decide for you. Ask people who know.
After a record week, stay level. Do not spend like it will last.
Hold yourself to a high standard no matter your title. Skip the show.
Before you give someone a new role, match it to their strengths.
Lead with the answer and stop. Busy people want it short.
Earn respect with skill. People who demand it have not earned it.
After a win, assume something still needs fixing. Go look for it.
Pair a fast worker with a careful one on hard jobs.
When someone makes a mistake, assume it was an honest slip first.
Retire a routine while it still works, before it fails you.
Do one good turn for someone each day. Friends build over time.
Earn trust early. People who trust you forgive a slow day.
In good times, save money and goodwill for the lean days.
Never run down rivals. Win on your own work.
Decide calmly which of your crew's habits matter. Let the rest go.
Pick partners by how they act, not by what the contract says.
Show the work, not yourself. Bragging and putting yourself down both fall flat.
Greet everyone with respect, even people who are against you. It costs little.
One rude remark can outlast a hundred good jobs. Watch your words.
Keep your methods up to date. Keep your word no matter what.
Let small troubles fade. Settle what matters early and drop the rest.
Explain calmly and show proof. That earns more respect than big talk.
Talk plainly. Trying too hard makes real skill look fake.
Be so good at your work that people miss you when you are gone.
When talk turns to other people's mistakes, steer it back to your own work.
Never hide a mistake from a customer. Fix it, learn, and move on.
Bring an easy, warm manner to hard talks. It helps more than you think.
On a bad week, keep the same standards you hold on a good one.
Do not complain to suppliers or crew. Talk about what works and what is next.
Show the worn part, explain it, and write it down. Unseen work does not count.
If someone who wronged you later needs help, treat them well.
When someone pushes for an answer now, say you will get back to them.
Do not chase odd ideas just to stand out. Use good sense with others.
Do not depend on one supplier or one source of leads. Keep a backup.
Push back when it matters. Do not argue every small point.
When a meeting drifts, ask the main question first.
Make choices from your own clear thinking, not from what others think.
When tempers run hot, step back and let things settle before you act.
If a task fails twice on a bad day, stop. Try again tomorrow.
Review someone's work by naming what they did well first.
When you explain something, watch their face, not your own words.
If a rival is right first, agree. Do not take the wrong side to oppose them.
Do not go odd just to avoid being plain. Aim to be good.
Start with what the other person wants. Then show how your offer helps them.
Keep your sore spots private. Do not vent your stress in public.
Do not trust the first story. Check it yourself before you judge.
Give someone you trust the right to tell you when you are wrong.
Match your tone to the person. Value care with words over fancy talk.
Take the blame yourself when a plan fails. Do not let your crew carry it.
Never call your own work cheap. Price it for what it is worth.
Plan for next season's trouble now. Fixing it with customers waiting costs more.
Hire people more skilled than you at their craft. Their good work lifts the whole business.
If you change how something is done, make the new way plainly better right away.
When a new vendor makes big promises, try them with a small order first.
If you must show anger, say why, set the line, and end it there.
Take advice from people whose judgment has held up over time, not just fun people.
When hiring, ask how they fixed a past mistake. That beats a smooth interview.
Ask each contact for help with what they know best. Stay in touch between favors.
When someone argues the obvious, stay calm. Your calm is what people will remember.
Tell customers what you know, not what you hope. They hear every word as a promise.
Name your favorite bad habit out loud. Ask someone you trust to call it out.
When someone talks you down, reply once, kindly. Let better work do the rest.
Help people in trouble with what you can spare. Never stake your business on saving theirs.
Try a new idea on a small scale first. Watch how people react, then decide.
In a dispute, stick to the facts. Never use what someone told you in trust.
Judge vendors and hires by what they deliver, not by their pitch.
In a bad week, list what you can control today and start on the first item.
Do not change a process that works just because you are bored with it.
One sloppy job can undo a hundred good ones. Check the last step every time.
Keep some cash, spare parts, and free time in reserve for the bad day.
Save big favors for real emergencies. Do not use one on a rush you saw coming.
Do not fight in public with someone who has nothing to lose. Reply once and stop.
Take criticism of your own calls without getting touchy. Then your crew can speak plainly too.
Work fast on the job list. Go slow on the rest of your life.
Only make claims you can back up today. Big promises that fall short hurt you later.
When a problem is outside your skill, ask a real expert early instead of guessing.
Be warm with your crew, but never let friendship decide pay or schedules.
If a deal looks good on paper but feels off, stop and work out why.
Keep your plans private. But tell each customer everything about their own car.
Do not announce your next move before it is ready. Plans are easy to copy.
Never lie to a customer. Choose kind words, but tell them all that affects their car.
Walk into meetings with big vendors as an equal. They need good customers too.
Hold the goal firm but the method loose. When facts prove you wrong, change.
Skip meetings no one needs. A quick word at the start of the day works better.
Do not bet everything on one big launch. Plan a few smaller pushes instead.
Hold big companies and yourself to the same rules you set for a new hire.
Give praise yourself, and give hard news yourself too. Do not make others carry it.
Pass along praise customers give your crew. Never win a sale by knocking another shop.
Never squeeze a stuck customer. Say so when a repair is safe to put off.
When you are swamped, note what broke down first. That is the next thing to fix.
Judge a vendor by their delivery record, not their charm. Keep your own promises too.
Let small slights pass. Save your energy and sleep for what matters.
When someone pitches a deal as a favor to you, ask who takes the risk.
Plan the realistic version first. Treat the big version as a bonus, not the deadline.
Ask the newest person on your team how they would do it. Use the best way.
Notice which jobs and customers you win easily. Focus on those, not on everyone.
If a partner keeps making mistakes that hit your customers, end the deal.
Neighbors may value your work less than strangers do. Judge its worth for yourself.
To win a bigger account, show your record, ask once clearly, and do not nag.
Always keep a next goal. But finish every customer's job all the way.
When things go wrong, check your own calls first before blaming the crew.
A plan counts once it runs and helps. Until then it is only words.
Study people who have real results to show, not the loudest ones.
Give easy jobs full care. Break hard jobs into one small step for today.
When a rival or troll takes a shot, skip the public fight. Keep doing good work.
A customer who mocks every other shop will likely mock yours. Stay polite and calm.
When someone pushes hard over a bill, answer slowly and calmly. Heated words get repeated.
When worry loops at night, write the real risk, pick the next step, and stop.
Do not assume rivals have it easier. Look at your own numbers instead.
When a car needs more work than hoped, tell the customer gently but leave nothing out.
Slow weeks and busy weeks are both normal. Keep the same routine through both.
Teach your crew everything you know. Keep learning so you always have more to teach.
Ask a vendor or tech why, then why again, to find the real reason.
Own a mistake and fix it at once. Covering it up creates a second one.
When a vendor opens with a sweet deal, read the terms that come after it.
When you give a task, say in one clear sentence what done looks like.
Keep private business details out of casual friendships. Leave room to make up with old rivals.
If someone shows you a better way, switch. Do not turn it into a contest.
Say what you mean. Your quote and your final bill should always match.
When a bigger rival outspends you, win with quick answers and good follow up, not tricks.
Skip small corrections. Save them for what matters and give them in private.
Keep undecided plans out of shop talk, so your crew does not chase rumors.
Keep your look and voice plain and steady. Let people remember the work, not a gimmick.
Read a bad review for what to fix, not only for how it stings.
Find the weak spot that sits next to your best strength. Work on that one first.
Give free, honest advice to people who are not buying today. They may come back later.
When a complaint comes in, hear the other side and check the notes before you judge.
Do not trash talk other shops or customers. Your crew copies your tone.
Set regular time to read, time to learn from others, and time to think ahead.
Check your numbers each week, even when things seem fine.
Show work only when it is done. Hand back every car clean and complete.
Know your costs, labor times, and supplier terms by heart, so no one can fool you.
Ask customers if they want the full details or just the short answer.
Put deals in writing and share the stakes, so partners have reason to keep their word.
Make a big request after things go well, not the day after a fight.
Invest in a promising worker early with training. It works best with people who repay trust.
Share private matters only with those who need to know. Do not pry into others' troubles.
Find the one skill your business lacks. Build it or give it to your strongest person.
When a debate turns into nitpicking, steer back to the one point that settles it.
Explain repairs in plain words. Speak simply, but never play dumb to dodge a fair question.
Laugh off jokes about you. Be careful with your own, since new people cannot push back.
Finish what you started before you begin something new.
Stay honest, but check any deal that seems too good or any urgent payment request.
Notice when someone makes you feel you owe them. Settle fairly and thank people plainly.
Keep people around who tell you when an idea is weak. Worry when everyone agrees.
Tell customers what they need. Do not stack nervous excuses on a fair bill.
Hand off chores that repeat. Keep your own hours for learning and big calls.
Keep the plan you made unless you can name a real reason to change it.
Do the work that brings in money first. Extras wait until that is done.
A buyer who knocks what they want may just want a lower price. Stick to facts.
Prepare as if it all depends on you. Then accept what you cannot control.
Help your crew in the rush, but keep some weekly hours that no one can take.
Explain every charge clearly, but skip details no one asked about.
Trace a small repeat problem to its cause right away, before more pile on.
Give small praise often. It builds more loyalty than one big gesture.
Agree ahead of time how to handle angry customers. Restate the facts calmly and politely.
When you must end a partnership, do it politely and in writing. Avoid a shouting match.
Bring your key people into big decisions early, so the choice is truly shared.
Reach out to a nearby rival. You might trade work that each of you does better.
Different people can know different parts of your business. Just never mislead anyone.
If a new process fails after a fair trial, stop it and say so.
After a bad day, write down what to fix once. Then let the rest go.
Before you buy a tool you will rarely use, price out renting it.
Run every day as if your toughest customer is about to walk in.
Give a good worker a harder job, with backup close by. See what they can do.
Being easygoing is fine, but not on safety. When something matters, let people see it.
Use a warm tone, but never let nice words hide a fact the customer needs.
Fix the weak spot now. It costs less than fixing it after it breaks.
When you launch something new, work hard in the first weeks. Have the follow up ready.
Before you dismiss a tool many good shops use, find out what they get from it.
On a job you do not know well, follow the proven steps or call an expert.
Keep the price firm. Clear answers and a polite handoff bring people back.
Notice if a customer is scared or doubtful. Explain the estimate the way they need.
Good work is not enough. Add a friendly greeting and easy talk.
Join your crew's jokes and outings, but stay the one who sets the rules.
Each year, pick one new skill to add. Give your people room to grow too.
Share real finished work one piece at a time, with permission. Skip the big boast.
Be known for honest work done well. Skip stunts that get attention but lose trust.
When a caller keeps pushing for inside details, stay polite and share nothing extra.
If other shops pad their bills, let that be your reason to keep yours honest.
Seek feedback from people who know the craft. Their quiet yes beats a crowd's likes.
Build a business that runs well when you are gone. Then step away and test it.
Test new ideas where mistakes are cheap. Keep repair calls on methods that are proven.
Follow up with past customers only when it helps them. Space it out and never push.
Help a struggling friend with advice, but do not take on their debts.
Set up your team so not every choice runs through you.
When a dispute heats up, pause or let someone else step in for a minute.
Let daily plans bend to what walks in. Keep honesty as the one fixed rule.
Avoid careless jokes in front of customers. Admitting a mistake builds trust instead of costing it.
You can be liked and respected. Stay warm, but hold the same standards every day.
Test a new hire on a real job and a new vendor on a small order.
Earn respect by your daily judgment and character, not by your title.
Stay calm and steady in a rush. Your crew reads that more than any speech.
When two of your people disagree, have each argue the other side before you decide.
Claim only what you truly do. Never buy fake reviews or puff up a result.
Pick a few big strengths, like being reliable and fair, and build them into everything.
Do hidden work as well as work the customer can see.
When things are unclear, list your options, test them hard, then pick with care.
Post less often but make each post worth reading. Too much makes people tune out.
Before profit or speed, ask if the plan is honest. Start every choice there.
